title: Are artists liars?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Shortly before his death, the Hollywood icon Marlon Brando made a series of instructional videos about acting, to be called 'Lying for a Living'. On the surviving footage, Brando can be seen dispensing advice to a group of enthusiastic, if somewhat bemused, Hollywood stars, including Leonardo Di Caprio and Sean Penn. 'If you can lie, you can act,' Brando said. He was not the first person to note that the line between an artist and a liar is a fine one. If art is a kind of lying, then lying is a form of art, albeit of a lower order – as the writers Oscar Wilde and Mark Twain have observed. Both liars and artists refuse to accept the tyranny of reality. Both carefully craft stories that are worthy of belief – a skill requiring intellectual sophistication, emotional sensitivity and physical self-control (liars are writers and performers of their own work).

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Such parallels are hardly coincidental, as I discovered while researching my book on lying. Indeed, lying and artistic storytelling spring from a common neurological root – one that is exposed in the cases of psychiatric patients who suffer from a particular kind of condition known as chronic confabulation. This is a rare type of memory problem that affects a small proportion of brain-damaged people. It is defined as: 'the production of fabricated memories about oneself or the world, without the conscious intention to deceive'. Chronic confabulation is usually associated with damage to the brain's frontal lobes, particularly the region responsible for self-regulation and self-censoring. Most of us control the way we voice our thoughts for the sake of truth, sense and social appropriateness. Chronic confabulators can't do this. They randomly combine real memories with stray thoughts, wishes and hopes, and summon up a story from the confusion.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Confabulating patients are nearly always oblivious to their own condition, and will give absurdly implausible explanations of what has happened to them. One patient, asked about his surgical scar, explained that during the second world war he surprised a teenage girl who shot him three times in the head, killing him, only for surgery to bring him back to life. Others tell yet more fantastical tales, about trips to the moon, or fighting alongside Alexander the Great (356–323 BC) in India. Confabulators aren't out to deceive. Instead, they are seized by a 'compulsion to narrate': a deep-seated need to shape, order and explain what they do not understand. The stories spun by chronic confabulators are conjured up instantaneously – an interlocutor only has to ask a question, or say a particular word, and they're off, like a jazz player doing an improvisation. Unlike jazz players, however, chronic liars have little or no control over their own material.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The wider significance of chronic confabulation is what it tells us about ourselves. Evidently there is a gushing river of verbal creativity in the normal human mind, from which both artistic invention and lying are drawn. We are born storytellers, spinning narrative out of our experience and imagination, straining against the leash that keeps us tethered to reality. This is a wonderful thing; it is what gives us our ability to conceive of alternative futures and other worlds. And it helps us to make sense of our own existence through the entertaining stories of others. But it can lead us into trouble, particularly when we try to persuade others that our inventions are real.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: During a now-famous libel* case in 1996, Jonathan Aitken, a former minister in the British government, attempted to clear his name following accusations by a national newspaper. The case, which stretched on for more than two years, involved a series of claims that, on a trip to Paris while he was a government minister, meetings had occurred between Aitken and a group of arms dealers. Aitken denied the claims, but his case collapsed in June 1997, when the defence found indisputable evidence about his Paris trip. Until then, Aitken's charm, fluency and flair for theatrical displays of sincerity looked as if they might bring him victory. What amazed many in hindsight was the sheer superfluity of the lies Aitken told during his testimony. Some were necessary to maintain his original lie, but others were told, it appeared, just for the enjoyment of it.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Of course, unlike Aitken, playwrights and novelists are not literally attempting to deceive us, because the rules are laid out in advance: come to the theatre, or open this book, and we'll lie to you. Perhaps this is why we felt it necessary to invent art in the first place: as a safe space into which our lies can be channelled into something socially useful. But that is not the whole story. The key way in which artistic 'lies' differ from normal lies, and from the 'honest lying' of chronic confabulators, is that they have a significance and resonance beyond their creator. The liar lies on behalf of himself; the artist tells lies on behalf of everyone. If writers have a compulsion to narrate, they compel themselves to find insights about the human condition. Art is a lie whose secret ingredient is truth.

groups.title: The case of Jonathan Aitken
content: A {{24}} accused a British politician called Jonathan Aitken of being in touch with people who were buying and selling {{25}} . Aitken took them to court, saying the accusations were untrue, but there was evidence that meetings had taken place in Paris, and he lost the case. Afterwards, many people commented that some of the lies he produced in court were told for his own {{26}} , and were actually unnecessary.

subtitle: Humans are natural-born storytellers, so lying is in our blood. Ian Leslie considers how this comes out in our art
footnotes: * libel: the act of writing or printing untrue statements about someone
